title: A Crush Fracture on Prednisolone / Protect the Bones, Never Stop the Steroid Suddenly

blocks.text: A Crush Fracture on Prednisolone / Protect the Bones, Never Stop the Steroid Suddenly

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-34 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: National Osteoporosis Guideline Group (NOGG): UK clinical guideline for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis, summary of main recommendations (2024; updated December 2024) · Related AMaC: None identified

Dear Doctor, a 69-year-old retired librarian. Sudden mid-back pain after a sneeze two weeks ago. X-ray shows a wedge fracture of a thoracic vertebra. Prednisolone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for five months. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A vertebral fracture after minimal trauma on long-term prednisolone is osteoporosis until another cause is found. The danger is in the advice: stopping the steroid suddenly can cause an adrenal crisis, and some fractures have other causes.

The Examiner Trap. She blames the prednisolone and wants to stop it today. Candidates agree, or give a bisphosphonate and forget the other causes. Pass: keep the steroid, exclude myeloma and cord compression, treat the bones. Fail: stop prednisolone.

rows: Ask about the pain and its red flags, then ask about the steroid, falls and her bone risk factors.
"Tell me about the pain. Any weakness, numbness or trouble passing urine? How long on prednisolone? Any falls?"
Pain; red flags; steroid dose and duration; falls; height loss; diet; smoking; alcohol; family history; fractures.
Check the spine and the legs, and look for height loss and other causes.
"May I look at your back and test the strength and feeling in your legs? Tell me if anything hurts."
Height; kyphosis; spinal tenderness; leg power; sensation; reflexes; gait; cushingoid signs; cover her.
Explain the diagnosis, the safe steroid advice, the tests and the bone treatment, and give warning signs.
"Your bones have thinned. Please keep taking prednisolone, we'll check your blood and start a bone-protecting tablet."
Tests; steroid unchanged; calcium and vitamin D; bisphosphonate; falls; red flags; review.
No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed.
Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her.
Also offers a chaperone and helps her to move without pain.
Asks about pain only; omits red flags, steroid duration or falls.
Asks red flags, steroid dose and duration, falls, height loss, diet, smoking, alcohol and family history of fracture.
Also asks about weight loss, night pain, previous fractures, menopause, reflux and dental work.
Omits the neurology; reports cord signs that are absent.
Finds height loss, a thoracic kyphosis, tenderness over one vertebra, normal leg power and sensation, and normal gait.
Also finds normal reflexes, no cushingoid signs and no bladder or bowel changes.
Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis with a vertebral fragility fracture.
Also excludes myeloma, metastases, hypercalcaemia, vitamin D deficiency, hyperthyroidism and hypogonadism.
Asks for a DXA scan, calcium, vitamin D, kidney function, myeloma screen and full blood count.
Also asks for thyroid function, liver function and ESR, and says treatment need not wait for DXA (NOGG 2024).
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): tells her to stop prednisolone herself, or starts a bisphosphonate before checking calcium and vitamin D.

Says continue prednisolone unchanged, correct calcium and vitamin D first, then bone-protective treatment chosen with a bone specialist because risk is very high (recent vertebral fracture on prednisolone 7.5 mg or more), and gives red flags for the back.
Also covers analgesia, how to take alendronate upright with water, urgent help for weakness or bladder change, and names anabolic therapy as the option a specialist may offer first.
Brushes aside her fear of the steroid and of future fractures.
Asks what worries her, acknowledges both and explains the steroid is needed and the bones can be protected.
Also addresses her fear of jaw problems from bisphosphonates honestly, and her fear of falling.
Tells her what to do with no choices.
Explains tablets weekly, or a yearly infusion, or doing nothing, and asks her choice.
Records her choice, arranges falls and physiotherapy review, and gives a written, dated plan.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 69-year-old retired librarian. You are quietly stoic, health-conscious and suspicious of long-term tablets.
Opening line: "I sneezed and heard something crack. I've read the steroids thin the bones, so I'd like to stop them today."
Volunteered: two weeks of mid-back pain, worse on standing. Prednisolone 10 mg for five months for polymyalgia rheumatica; the stiffness is much better.
Only if asked about red flags: no leg weakness, numbness or bladder or bowel change. No weight loss. Some night pain.

Only if asked: you have lost about 3 cm in height. No previous fractures. A glass of wine most evenings. Your mother broke her hip at 78. You take no calcium or vitamin D. You have mild reflux. You have never smoked. You take no other regular medicines and have no allergies. No recent travel. You live alone in a bungalow.

Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are frightened of falling and ending up in a care home like your mother. A friend told you bone tablets rot the jaw. Say: "I don't want any tablet that wrecks my teeth."
Your questions, in your own words: "Can I stop the steroids?" "Why did my bones go?" "Are the bone tablets safe?"
How you react: if told to stop prednisolone, you do. If listened to and told to continue, with a plan, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: comfortable sitting; pulse 76 regular; blood pressure 136/82; temperature 36.7 °C. Height 3 cm below her recorded height. Mild thoracic kyphosis; tenderness over one thoracic vertebra. Leg power, sensation and reflexes normal; gait normal. No cushingoid features.

Results, only when requested: calcium normal; vitamin D low; kidney function normal; blood count normal; myeloma screen negative; ESR consistent with polymyalgia rheumatica. DXA: osteoporosis at the spine.
Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. What else must you exclude? (D) 3. Which tests first? (E) 4. Which treatment? (E) 5. Why is stopping prednisolone dangerous? (E)

Curveballs: She asks to stop prednisolone: no, adrenal crisis risk; the rheumatology team reduces it. She has new leg weakness and urinary retention: emergency. She declines tablets: discuss infusion.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks red flags, steroid duration, falls and height loss (C)
Examines the spine and the legs' power, sensation and gait (A)
Finds height loss, kyphosis, one tender vertebra and normal neurology (B)
Names glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis with a vertebral fracture (D)
Excludes myeloma, metastases and other secondary causes (D)
Requests DXA, calcium, vitamin D, kidney function and a myeloma screen (E)
Says continue prednisolone and replace vitamin D before a bisphosphonate (E)
Gives red flags for cord compression and falls advice (E)
Recognises very high fracture risk and refers to a bone specialist (E)
Asks what worries her and addresses the steroid and jaw fears (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Sit up. [R1 Fail] Back hurt? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Presses the spine, no neurology.) [R3 Fail] A strain. [R4 Fail] Repeat the X-ray. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Stop the prednisolone. [R6 Fail] Don't worry. [R7 Fail] See your GP. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): stopping prednisolone suddenly risks an adrenal crisis. No consent, no neurology, a fracture called a strain, and her fears dismissed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I look at your back and test your legs? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]

CANDIDATE: Any weakness, numbness or bladder trouble? How long on prednisolone? Any falls or height loss? Do you smoke or drink alcohol, what is your diet like, and has anyone in the family broken a hip? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: No weakness. Five months. I've lost 3 cm.
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Height loss, a kyphosis, one tender vertebra, normal legs and gait. Thank you; I've covered you. [R3 Pass] [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis with a vertebral fracture; myeloma and other causes must be excluded. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: A DXA scan, calcium, vitamin D, kidney function, a blood count and a myeloma screen. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: Keep taking prednisolone unchanged. Correct vitamin D first. Your recent spinal fracture on prednisolone puts you at very high risk, so I will refer you to the bone specialists to choose the best treatment; we do not need to wait for the DXA to start protecting your bones. Leg weakness or bladder change means urgent help. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: Falling, and bone tablets damaging my teeth.

CANDIDATE: Both are fair. The steroid is needed, and your bones can be protected. [R7 Pass] We can use weekly tablets or a yearly infusion, or you could choose to have no bone treatment, which leaves a high risk of another fracture. Which do you prefer? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Kept the steroid, excluded other causes and gave a safety net. Did not name the wider causes or give alendronate instructions.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll help you move gently. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any weight loss, night pain, previous fractures, the menopause, reflux or dental work? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Normal reflexes, no cushingoid signs, no bladder or bowel change. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis; I'd also exclude myeloma, metastases, hypercalcaemia, vitamin D deficiency and hyperthyroidism. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: The tests, plus thyroid and liver function and ESR. We needn't wait for the DXA to treat. [R5 High]

CANDIDATE: Prednisolone unchanged; rheumatology will reduce it. Alendronate upright with water, and your reflux needs checking. Because a recent spinal fracture on prednisolone puts you at very high risk, the bone specialists may offer an anabolic treatment first; alendronate is the usual alternative. Weakness or bladder change means 999. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: Jaw problems are rare, and a dental check helps. I'll refer you for falls assessment and physiotherapy. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a review date. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, wider history, secondary causes, tests, alendronate and reflux advice, an honest jaw answer, falls referral and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about red flags. Cord compression and cancer present with back pain, and they need action today.
R4: Calling it a strain. A vertebral fracture on steroids is osteoporosis until another cause is found, and myeloma must be excluded.
R6: Telling her to stop prednisolone. Sudden withdrawal after months can cause an adrenal crisis.
R6: Starting a bisphosphonate without correcting vitamin D. Low calcium can follow treatment.
"Can I check your legs and ask about bladder or bowel changes?"
"I should exclude other causes of a fracture before giving a diagnosis."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

NOGG 2024: offer treatment to people at high and very high fracture risk. Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate or risedronate) or intravenous zoledronate are first-line; denosumab is an alternative. A vertebral fracture within the last 2 years, or oral prednisolone 7.5 mg daily or more for 3 months, marks very high risk: consider referral to an osteoporosis specialist, as some people need anabolic treatment first.

Glucocorticoids: with prednisolone 7.5 mg daily or more for 3 months, start bone protection at the same time without waiting for DXA (NOGG 2024). Ensure sufficient dietary calcium and vitamin D, and supplement if needed.

Plan oral bisphosphonates for at least 5 years, or intravenous zoledronate for at least 3 years, then reassess fracture risk; longer courses are needed for people on high-dose oral glucocorticoids or with a vertebral fracture (NOGG 2024).
THINK: Fracture on steroids: osteoporosis; exclude myeloma.
SAY: "Your bones have thinned; keep taking prednisolone."
DO: Ask red flags; check legs; do not stop steroid.
NUMBERS: Prednisolone 7.5 mg or more for 3 months: protect bones; recent vertebral fracture: very high risk (NOGG 2024).
TRAP: Stopping steroid; skipping vitamin D.
FINISH: Calcium, vitamin D, specialist referral for bone treatment, falls, red flags.
